To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high density lipoproten (HDL) subclasses, HDL2 and 3 protect low density lipoproteins (LDL) against oxidative modification by inhibiting the formation of reactive oxygen species.
HDL2 and 3 are effective antioxidants and scavengers of free radicals and thus protect LDL from oxidative modifications.
HDL subclasses inhibit LDL oxidation by scavenging oxygen derived free radicals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the antioxidant properties of the HDL subclasses in vitro and their potential role in the prevention of atherogenesis.
the protective role of HDL subclasses in preventing the oxidative modifications in low density lipoproteins.
the protective effects of HDL subclasses against LDL-oxidation in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HDL subclasses are potent scavengers of free radicals and thus protect LDL from oxidation.
HDL3 is a better protector against LDL oxidation in vitro.
HDL3 is a more potent scavenger of OH- and HDL2 is a better antioxidant of LDL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, HDL subclasses are the potent scavenger against the oxygen derived free radicals and protect LDL from oxidative degradation.
HDL2 and 3 inhibit the oxidation of LDL lipids and protein by nonenzymic and enzymic systems in vitro and the protection offered by HDL subclasses was comparable to that of alpha-tocopherol.
HDL3 is a better antioxidant than HDL2, which is more effective than tocopherol.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HDL subclasses are the potent inhibitors of LDL oxidation and may be used as a preventive measure in the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis.
HDL subclasses are the most important scavengers of free radicals and protect LDL from oxidation in non enzymic system in vitro.
HDL2 is more potent in inhibiting LDL oxidation than HDL3.
